1601-conversation-as-it-was-by-the-socia:
Mark Twain imagines an evening in the time of the Tudors, when great ladies and gentlemen sit by the fire and talk with a frankness no Victorian drawing room allowed. The introduction quotes his own scratch-pad line: born irreverent, he hoped to remain so. It also tells how he once sent the piece, unsigned, to an editor who had cried out for a new Rabelais — and got it savagely abused.

The talk ranges over the customs, learning, and scandal of Queen Elizabeth's court, in language Twain delighted to make as broad as the age itself. He printed the sketch privately for friends in his lifetime. It stands as his bawdiest jeu d'esprit, learned and improper in equal measure.
19900-the-mysteries-of-all-nations-rise-:
James Grant's Mysteries of All Nations traces the rise and progress of superstition. He confesses his examples come from an almost unlimited number. Many interesting particulars had to be omitted, he says. A friend's letter from Macroom, Ireland, arrived even as the last sheet was revised. It corroborated his Irish material handsomely. Grant piles custom upon custom across nations and centuries.

Victorian rationalists loved cataloging the beliefs they opposed. Charms, omens, witch trials, and holy frauds fill such surveys. Grant writes as a journalist, brisk and anecdotal. Modern readers can mine him for folklore he scorned. Ireland, Scotland, and farther lands all supply cases. The book is a museum of nineteenth-century unbelief.
20191-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
J. E. Bygate wrote the Bell's Cathedrals volume on the cathedral church of Durham. Bygate draws much of the account from his own time in the building. He also used Greenwell's pamphlet and Ross's County of Durham. Those sources add depth on one of England's greatest Norman churches.

Durham Cathedral crowns its rock above the River Wear in bold mass. The book describes its nave, shrine, towers, and long past in order. Bell's series made each great church plain to tourists and students. Readers get a compact guide rich in stone, story, and saint lore.
20641-through-three-campaigns-a-story-of:
G. A. Henty built his boys' novel Through Three Campaigns out of three real British campaigns. The relief of Chitral, the Tirah campaign, and the relief of Coomassie in Ashanti supply the action. Henty's heroes serve as young officers and learn soldiering on three frontiers.

The first two campaigns, Henty notes, were fought in mountainous country. The ground gave every advantage to the enemy, since passes had to be scaled and torrents crossed under fire. The Ashanti fighting moved through forest instead. Henty mixes exact military detail with adventure, in the style that made him the boys' historian of the empire.
20810-the-ladies-of-llangollen-as-sketch:
About 1778, two ladies quit gay society to seek a secluded life together. Their search for a fitting spot led them to Llangollen in Wales. There they planned days of friendship, charity, and quiet good works.

Lady Eleanor Butler and Sarah Ponsonby became famed as the Ladies of Llangollen. Poets, lords, and travellers beat a path to their cottage door. This sketch, drawn by many hands, gathers views of their odd, admired life. Readers meet two women who built a celebrated home on their own terms, against the grain of their age.
20832-campfire-girls-at-twin-lakes-or-th:
Laughter, a bit scornful, greets Katherine Crane's riddle-like speech at Twin Lakes. Eleven girls of Flamingo Camp Fire form an arc on the grass before her. White tents dot the hillside camp in this Campfire Girls tale.

A summer vacation quest drives the plot, with lake, woods, and camp craft in play. Stella Francis, who wrote such tales, filled them with hikes and good deeds. The Camp Fire movement's laws of health and service shape each scrape. Young readers got both fun and a model of sturdy, kind girlhood in these brisk outdoor tales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acta-pilati:
Acta Pilati, or the Gospel of Nicodemus, does not claim Pilate as author, but claims descent from official acts kept in the praetorium at Jerusalem. Its alleged Hebrew original is attributed to Nicodemus, while the title Gospel of Nicodemus is medieval. The apocryphon won wide credit in the Middle Ages and greatly shaped legends of the Passion. Its popularity shows in its many languages, each with two or more recensions: Greek, Coptic, Armenian, and Latin.

The Acta fall into three sections of uneven style. The first covers the trial of Jesus, based on Luke 23. The second covers the Resurrection. An appendix on the descent to hell is absent from the Greek text and later added. In it Leucius and Charinus, souls raised after the Crucifixion, tell the Sanhedrin of the Lord's descent to Limbo. Eusebius, well informed in 325, is cited on the work, and Lipsius and Dobschutz supply modern study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-sc:
Alessandro Scarlatti was a Sicilian-born composer, born in 1659 at Trapani or Palermo and dead at Naples in October 1725. His tomb calls him music's restorer, and the entry credits him with originating the classical style of the eighteenth century and advancing concerted instrumental music. His first opera of 1679, Gli Equivoci nel Sembiante, was performed for Queen Christina of Sweden, and his career moved between Rome and Naples.

Scarlatti wrote more than a hundred operas, less than half surviving. He also wrote oratorios, motets, and innumerable chamber cantatas and serenades, plus organ, harpsichord, and other instrumental music. After serving at Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome, he returned to Naples in 1708 or 1709 and lived there ten years. He then lived in Rome from 1718 to 1721 before dying at Naples. His distinction was to lay the foundation of the new style later perfected by Neapolitan and German composers, including Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alesso-baldov:
Alesso Baldovinetti was a Florentine painter, born in Florence in October 1427, dead there in August 1499. Born to a wealthy merchant father, he left the business and joined the Academy of St. Luke at twenty-one. He called himself a pupil of Paolo Uccello and, according to Vasari, taught the famous Ghirlandaio. He experimented with colour in fresco and oil, though his works survive badly preserved, and he ranked as his day's best mosaic worker.

Baldovinetti helped Andrea del Castagno and Domenico Veneziano with the lost frescoes of Santa Maria Nuova in Florence. Surviving works include a large Adoration of the Shepherds in the cloisters of Sant'Annunziata and the design for Domenico del Michelino's portrait of Dante in the duomo. His Holy Trinity Adored by Saints Gualberto and Benedetto, painted for Santa Trinità, now hangs in the Florence Academy. His Annunciation and Enthroned Virgin and Child hang in the Uffizi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-alciat:
Andrea Alciati, an Italian jurist, was born at Alzano, near Milan, in 1492 and died at Pavia in 1550. The only son of a Milanese ambassador to Venice, he studied law at Pavia and Bologna. In 1522 he published Paradoxa juris civilis, an explanation of the Greek terms in Roman law, a work he had composed at fifteen.

He became professor of law at Avignon in 1518, then at Bourges, and returned to Milan in 1538 as professor at Pavia, teaching at Milan, Bologna, and Ferrara. Paul III and Charles V honoured him as the first scholar of his age to dress barbarous legal learning with literary skill. His jurisprudence was collected at Padua in 1571 in six folio volumes, beside a posthumous history of Milan, his Responsa, a formula of the Roman empire, and epigrams. Today his Emblemata, metrical moral sayings in elegant diction, first edited at Augsburg in 1531, is his best-known work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anima-christi:
The Anima Christi is a well-known prayer from the early fourteenth century, enriched with indulgences by Pope John XXII in 1330. All manuscripts agree on these facts, so there can be no doubt of their exactness. As to authorship, it was perhaps written by John XXII. This is uncertain, since this pope has been falsely credited with similar compositions.

The prayer was long believed to be Saint Ignatius Loyola's, since he puts it in his Spiritual Exercises and often refers to it. This is a mistake: it appears in prayer books of the saint's youth and manuscripts before his birth in 1491. James Mearns found it in a British Museum manuscript of 1370. A prayer book of Cardinal Peter de Luxembourg, dead in 1387, contains it. The prayer was so well known in Ignatius's time that he only mentions it in the first edition, while later editions print it in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-lotti:
Venetian composer Antonio Lotti, born in 1667 and dead there in 1740, studied under Legrenzi and produced an opera, Il Giustino, written in his sixteenth year. He became second organist of St. Mark's in 1692, first organist in 1704, and maestro di cappella, or music director, in 1736, beating strong rivals for a post paying 400 ducats. Between 1703 and 1730 he wrote many masses and motets, short sacred choral pieces, above all a Miserere that replaced Legrenzi's setting and is still sung at St. Mark's each Holy Thursday.

He also wrote twenty-seven operas between 1693 and 1717 and spent two years at Dresden. After returning to Venice in November 1719, he abandoned secular writing and devoted himself to church and chamber music alone. A disputed madrigal, a part song, that Bononcini claimed as his own forms a famous incident, now generally judged to have wronged Bononcini.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aporti:
Italian educator and theologian Ferrante Aporti, born at San Martino dell'Argine in 1791 and dead at Turin in 1858, pioneered infant schools in Italy. After ordination and three years of study at Vienna, he became professor of church history at the Cremona seminary and superintendent of schools there. His special care was the schooling of poor children, and in 1827 he opened an infant school at Cremona for their benefit.

Success led to similar schools in other Italian cities, which Aporti visited in person. He encouraged teachers and published guides for them, including a manual for infant schools in 1833 and a primer in 1837. At the University of Turin he taught a course on teaching methods that drew many teachers. France made him a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour in 1846, Victor Emmanuel made him a senator in 1848, and in 1855 he became rector of Turin University.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asti:
Asti, one of the districts of the region of Alexandria and suffragan of Turin, is a very old town that became Christian early in the Christian era. Its first known bishop was Pastor in 451, followed by Majoranus in 465, Benenatus in 680, and Evasius in 730. From 800 the regular bishops' list begins, though the see stood vacant from 1857 to 1867.

Some controversy surrounds the diocese's beginning and Evasius's episcopate, once placed by some at much older dates. Asti counts 182,600 Catholics, 107 parishes, and 300 secular priests, twelve regulars, ninety-two seminarians, and 525 churches or chapels. The entry is a compact diocesan record, joining an ancient town, a disputed early bishop, and a modern roll of parishes and clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-gabriel-po:
Blessed Gabriel Possenti, a Passionist student famed for holiness, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Assisi in 1838 as Francesco, son of Sante Possenti, he was baptised on his birth day and schooled by the Christian Brothers and Jesuits at Spoleto. After finishing secular study he joined the Passionists in 1856.

Clothed in the habit as Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows, he lived a short, intense religious life at Isola di Gran Sasso, dying in 1862 at twenty-three. Miracles reported at his tomb spread his fame. The entry presents a young student whose brief life became a model of devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-andre: Blessed Andrea Dotti, a Servite friar, was born in 1256 at Borgo San Sepolcro in Tuscany and died there in 1315. Brother of Count Dotto Dotti, captain of Philip the Fair's bodyguard archers, Andrea grew up a nobleman noted for piety and courage in the field. In 1278 a sermon by St. Philip Benizi at the Servite general chapter moved him to ask for the habit at once, and he rose by piety and learning in the order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-colom:
Blessed Colomba of Rieti, a Dominican mystic, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Rieti in Umbria in 1467, she died at Perugia in 1501, spending most of her life away from her birthplace. Her fame rested on two things: the highly miraculous cast of her career from its start, and her deep love for the Blessed Sacrament.

She belongs to a band of saintly Dominican women raised up, the entry says, as a contrast to the irreligion of Renaissance Italy. Visions, fasting, and counsel to cities marked her short life. The entry presents a young woman whose holiness challenged a corrupt age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capuciati:
Capuciati takes its name from the caputium, or hood, worn as a mark by two very different groups. The first was a short-lived peace confraternity founded in France in 1182 or 1183. Durand, a poor carpenter from Le Puy, claimed a vision of the Virgin Mary, who gave him a picture and inscription calling for peace. Members bound themselves to keep and procure peace, wearing a white hood and a medal with the image.

Centered at Our Lady's church in Le Puy, the movement spread swiftly south of the Loire before fading. The same name later marked a class of English Lollards who followed the preaching of Peter Pateshull around 1387. They kept their hoods on before the Blessed Sacrament, a gesture of defiance that gave them the old name in a new cause.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-giusepp:
Carlo Giuseppe Imbonati was a Cistercian of the Reform of St. Bernard, an orientalist, biographer, and theologian born at Milan. He flourished in the later seventeenth century, and his death date is disputed, though it certainly fell no earlier than 1696. He held the chairs of theology and Hebrew at Rome and rose to abbot, after studying under Giulio Bartolocci of the same order.

Bartolocci had planned the great rabbinical library, and Imbonati, his pupil turned collaborator, finished and edited its fourth volume at Rome in 1693. A supplementary fifth volume followed in 1694, with a chronology of Scripture and two dissertations on the Messiah and on Christ's divinity and humanity. His tragic chronicle of princes, dated from the St. Bernard monastery in April 1696, gives the last firm date of his career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cayes-haiti:
Cayes is a Haitian diocese, suffragan to Port-au-Prince. The province of Port-au-Prince, with its archdiocese and four suffragan dioceses, dates only from the reorganization after the Concordat of 1860. That agreement joined Pius IX and Haiti. Yet the faith had been planted in this part of Santo Domingo toward the end of the fifteenth century. Despite the island's political and social upheavals, it was never quite extinguished there.

The Bishop of Cayes, Jean-Marie-Alexandre Morice, elected in March 1893, governed the whole civil Department of the South from his see at Cayes, a seaport in the island's extreme southwest. The diocese counted 25 parishes with 500,000 people, almost all Catholics by profession, and in 1907 it held 95 churches or chapels served by 35 secular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celestino-sfo:
Celestino Sfondrati was prince-abbot of St. Gall and cardinal, born at Milan on 10 January 1644 and dying at Rome on 4 September 1696. He belonged to the noble Milanese Sfondrati family, which also produced Pope Gregory XIV and Cardinals Francesco and Paolo Sfondrati. At twelve he entered the Benedictine school at Rorschach, and on 26 April 1660 he took the habit at St. Gall.

By twenty-two he was already teaching philosophy and theology at Kempten. After ordination in 1668 he taught as professor and guided novices at his monastery. He taught canon law at Salzburg from 1679 to 1682, accepted the bishopric of Novara only with reluctance in 1686, and was instead elected prince-abbot of St. Gall in 1687. As abbot he modeled piety and mortification, and as prince he ruled mildly and won his people by great charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chieti:
The Archdiocese of Chieti, ancient Teate, capital of the Marrucini, stands on a mountain above the River Pescara in the Abruzzi of central Italy. Its people, once enemies of Rome, made a league with the Romans in 304 before Christ. They became a municipality after the Allied War and passed through Goths, Lombards, and Normans into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Saint Justinus is honoured as the first bishop, and the cathedral bears his name.

Among later bishops, Giovanni Pietro Caraffa resigned the see in 1524 to found the Theatine Order with Saint Cajetan, and later became Pope Paul the Fourth. Since 1525 Chieti has been an archbishopric without suffragans, or subordinate dioceses. It counts 300,500 people, 113 parishes, and 442 churches and chapels. Its clergy number 170 secular and 58 regular priests, and the bronze doors at Saint Clement's still show Bishop Gribaldus of 874.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cincinnati:
An entry on the Archdiocese of Cincinnati, covering southern Ohio across 12,043 square miles, erected as a see in June 1821 and raised to an archdiocese in July 1850. Jesuits crossed Ohio as early as 1749, a mission rose at Sandusky in 1751, and French settlers built a church at Gallipolis in 1790. Bishop Flaget of Bardstown, touring northern Ohio with Father Badin, found the first Catholics at Somerset and called the Dominicans to their aid.

Father Fenwick, later the first Bishop of Cincinnati, first offered Mass for thirteen families in John Fink's house at Somerset. He secured three hundred acres from the Dittoe family for a Dominican church and monastery. John Baptist Purcell, consecrated second bishop in October 1833, built a cathedral and seminary as numbers grew. William Henry Elder succeeded in 1880, Henry Moeller followed as coadjutor in 1903, and by Elder's death in 1904 the see counted 180,000 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coluccio-di-p:
Paul Lejay's entry follows Coluccio di Pierio di Salutati, an Italian humanist born in Tuscany in 1331 and dead on 4 May 1406. He studied at Bologna, then went to Rome to serve as pontifical secretary to Urban IV. He loved ancient letters. From 1368 he wrote to Petrarch. In 1375 Florence called him as chancellor of the republic. He held that office until his death. His life filled with politics, and he wrote against the Duke of Milan.

Salutati's learning also shaped the young. He met scholars at San Spirito convent and at the Alberti villa of Paradiso, around Luigi de' Marsiglii. He guided young men well, treating Poggio as a son and protecting Bruni. His works include short treatises on fate and fortune and on religion and flight from the world. Only De nobilitate legum et medicinae reached print, at Venice. His letters and learning mark a bridge to the Renaissance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniele-farla:
A biographical entry presents Daniele Farlati, an ecclesiastical historian born at San Daniele del Friuli in 1690 and dead in 1773. Schooled at Gorz, he joined the Jesuits at Bologna in 1707, taught classics at Padua for five years, and was ordained at Rome in 1722. Sent back to Padua, he assisted Filippo Riceputi on a planned ecclesiastical history of Illyria.

For twenty years the pair searched libraries and archives of ancient Illyria, filling three hundred manuscript volumes. Riceputi died in 1712, just as two large sections neared completion, leaving Farlati alone to shape the mass. With Jacopo Coleti as helper, he issued the first volume of Illyricum Sacrum at Venice in 1751. Three more followed before his death, and Coleti completed the eight-folio work in 1818.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-musti: Musti was a city of ancient Numidia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Roman Africa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niccolo-alber: Cardinal Niccolo Albergati was the Carthusian bishop-diplomat who served the papacy at the Council of Basel and across Europe. nasa-tm-19640008376-radio-frequency-elec:
Marshall Space Flight Center issued this standard, MSFC-STD-28, on June 26, 1963. It sets how to measure radio frequency shielding for equipment enclosures. Such boxes hold electrical gear in spacecraft checkout areas. The standard's foreword ties it to limits on stray electromagnetic noise.

Checkout areas need all systems to stay within set interference limits. Gear in those areas makes electromagnetic disturbance by its very nature, the foreword notes. A shielded enclosure cuts that noise down to safe levels. This standard fixes how the blocking power, called attenuation, gets measured. Uniform measures let every contractor's box be judged by the same fair test.
nasa-tm-19640014015-results-from-the-imp:

Serbu says the flat sensor measured energy spectra for ions and electrons. Energies ran from zero to a stated upper limit. Density measures were taken from low altitude out to many Earth radii. The results show a sharp drop in particle density at one distance. That drop matched a drop deduced from whistler observations. Electrons close to Earth showed calm, thermal energies in the data.
nasa-tm-19650003013-quality-control-and-:
Alfred J Babecki of NASA Goddard wrote this paper on quality control for scientific satellites. His concern is failure prevention. He stresses testing that does not destroy the part being tested, called nondestructive testing.

Babecki opens by urging everyone in the space program to feel responsible for a first-class product. He then discusses the role of the contractor in that work. The point is practical: a satellite cannot be repaired after launch. Careful checks on the ground are the main defense against failure in orbit. His argument is aimed at habits and attitudes as much as at test methods, which gives the paper a wider reach.
nasa-tm-19650011878-inter-sensory-judgme:

nasa-tm-19670002049-observations-of-the-:
Norman F. Ness, of the Laboratory for Space Sciences at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, wrote this August 1966 paper. It presents observations of how the solar wind meets Earth's magnetic field. Ness limits the paper to quiet conditions, the steady state rather than storms.

His introduction recalls how thinking on the subject changed. The Sun was once thought to emit ionized gas only briefly after solar flares. Work by Chapman, Ferraro, Chamberlain, and Parker built the idea of a steady outflow instead. Satellite measurements of magnetic storms fed that shift, and Ness sets his quiet-time observations against it.
nasa-tm-19670009415-lunar-occultation-an:
Larry W. Brown, of the Laboratory for Space Sciences at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, used the Moon as a shutter in this August 1966 paper. He observed the radio source MSH 21-23 during a lunar occultation. That is the moment the Moon passes in front of the source and cuts its signal off.

The observation was made on June 18, 1965, at NASA's Data Acquisition Facility. A large parabolic antenna tracked the center of the Moon, using a switched receiver with gain modulation. Timing the cutoff pinned down the source. The occultation gave position and diameter measurements, and a possible optical counterpart to the radio source.
nasa-tm-19670029763-intercomparison-of-c:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland issued this comparison in September 1967. It checks two tracking systems against each other on the GEOS-A geodetic satellite. One system ranged by laser light; the other, called GRARR, ranged by radio. Both tracked the same passes from the same area, so their results could be compared directly.

Seventeen passes were observed from July to November 1966 by the Rosman, North Carolina, stations, and ten were evaluated. Laser tracks, smoothed by a data adjustment program, served as the reference orbit. Against that standard, laser orbits exposed systematic errors in the radio system's range and range rate readings. Most passes showed a modest average range bias, while three outlier passes drifted far from it. Timing errors in both range and range rate were also measured. The authors attribute the range bias and timing faults to inaccuracies in the spacecraft transponder's delay curve.
nasa-tm-19690025755-galvanic-corrosion-a:
Galvanic Corrosion and Cathodic Protection is a selective bibliography prepared by the Kennedy Space Center Library. Librarian L. B. Russell and library chief R. A. Lindemann approved it on January 23, 1969. Its preface calls Cape Kennedy a corrosion engineer's paradise, battered by salt air, salt water, heat, and damp from every side.

Galvanic corrosion strikes where unlike metals meet and form a cell, the preface explains. Cathodic protection answers by making the guarded metal cathodic, with anodes that waste away or with applied current. One cited example protects the Vehicle Assembly Building's foundation pilings. Entries run in title order, drawn from abstract journals of the past six years. Each listing, per the report record, carries a short abstract.
nasa-tm-19700009492-traction-drive-syste:
Clyde S. Jones Jr., Billy J. Doran, and Frank J. Nola of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on November 25, 1969. It works through design choices for the drive system of a lunar roving vehicle. The drive had to move astronauts across the Moon's rough surface.

For a sound design, the authors weigh weight, energy use, and flexibility with the power supply, motor, and power train. They take up motor heat, the choice of alternating or direct current, and controllers that switch large currents. They also cover torque at changing speeds, braking that returns energy, and shifts in supply voltage.
nasa-tm-19700021193-reflection-coefficie:
Capers Rembert Cockrell wrote this master's thesis at George Washington University in February 1970. It studies horn antennas that radiate into dielectric materials. A dielectric is a material that does not conduct current but passes electric fields.

Cockrell works out formulas for how the horn opening behaves when covered by such a material. He treats the electric field inside the guide as a main wave plus one higher wave. His results cover the pyramidal horn and the H-plane horn. Antenna designers use reflection values like these to match a horn to the material it must beam into.
nasa-tm-19700021718-on-the-integrability:
Abolghasem Ghaffari of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in February 1970. It treats the cases where the motion equation for a satellite can be solved in full, closed form. The satellite moves in a gravity field that stays the same all the way around one axis.

Ghaffari works with the orbit's shadow on a plane set square to that axis of spin. He investigates two cases in which the governing equation can actually be integrated. In one, the work reduces to quadratures; in the other, to a simpler first-order equation. He also gives the equation's analytic and physical meaning, and shows it can be derived from the eikonal equation of geometric optics.
nasa-tm-19700026278-determination-of-lem:
An aerospace engineer in the Theoretical Mechanics Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center wrote this Apollo paper. It presents a way to fix the position of an unknown lunar landing site from the command module in orbit. The fix is made before the landing module leaves for the surface.

Two sightings of the site, taken a few minutes apart, feed the method. An optical tool measures each sighting angle against the craft's guidance platform. The crew could do the full computation on board, the paper states. The method also predicts the error in the fix. An example works the numbers through.
nasa-tm-19700026558-development-plan-for:
NASA issued this development plan for a voice communication system simulator. A simulator would let engineers test voice links on the ground before flight. It would copy the delays, noise, and limits that crews meet on real missions, so equipment could be tuned against them safely.

The plan opens with the concept, born of Apollo voice system testing on the ground. Engineers had learned that good voice design turns on many factors, starting with how voice operated relays behave. System description and design specifications follow, with charts of the system sequence and its gain control behavior. A bar graph schedule then lays out the development program step by step.
nasa-tm-19710027945-terrestrial-and-luna:
Paul D. Lowman Jr. of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in September 1971, numbered X-644-71-360, comparing Mars with Earth and the Moon. Mariner 6 and 7 photographs had just revealed Martian craters, channels, and broken ground in detail. Lowman matched those features against orbital photographs of Earth and Moon features of similar size.

He found five general categories of similarity. The Hellas basin reads as a tectonic basin filled with wind-blown sand, structurally like the basin under the Gulf of Mexico. Mars's chaotic terrain resembles crustal collapse seen in the Mojave Desert and the Afar depression. Other matches cover wind-blown sand deposits and crater dunes suggesting a northeast to southwest wind. Still others are ridges identical to those in lunar maria, hinting the Martian crust may be volcanic.
nasa-tm-19720023494-chemical-research-pr:
D. A. Kourtides and J. A. Parker wrote this NASA memorandum at Ames Research Center in September 1972. Ames sits at Moffett Field in California. Their report explains what the Chemical Research Projects Office did, what it had done, and what it planned next.

Short sections cover the office purpose and its main gains. Other sections describe its working groups, including an engineering test group and a polymer group. The report also names chemical research needed for urgent national problems tied to flight and space. Managers could read it as a compact record of one NASA chemistry office at work.
podcast-joerogan-_EWCN3CPhTI:
Eric Weinstein's episode 1320 of the Joe Rogan Experience is an early marathon in his run of visits. Weinstein came to lay out Geometric Unity, his bid for a unified theory of physics, and his charge that the field had rotted from within. Both themes define his later fame.

He tells Rogan how the theory began, why he sat on it for years, and what he thinks healthy science would look like. Rogan, then new to Weinstein's world, asks for the basics and gets manifestos. The episode is the seed of the Portal era that followed, kept as the fullest early record of Weinstein's case.
podcast-tuckercarlson-cUoO46OOztI:
Actor Jonathan Roumie joins Tucker Carlson to talk about playing Jesus in the hit show The Chosen. The title also names Christian martyrs and the power of Lent. Roumie speaks as a man whose own faith grew with the role.

Roumie shares tales from the set and how crowds react to him as the face of Jesus. He talks about prayer, fasting, and the cost of faith in lands where it can mean death. Carlson draws out the role faith plays in his daily life. Listeners get a warm, deep talk with an actor in a one of a kind role.
review-of-the-work-of-mr-john-stuart-mil:
George Grote, author of a history of ancient Greece, reviewed John Stuart Mill's Examination of Sir William Hamilton's Philosophy in a piece reprinted from the Westminster Review of January 1, 1866. The review was issued as a book in 1868. Mill's work, from Longmans in 1865, ran to twenty-eight chapters and five hundred and sixty pages.

Grote warns that no full abstract can fit his space, for Mill wastes no word. The book sets two great English thinkers face to face, Hamilton and Mill. Hamilton's Edinburgh lectures on logic and metaphysics had shaped a generation of students for twenty years. Grote, no follower of Hamilton, still grants his wide and lasting influence.
school-history-of-north-carolina-from-15:
John W. Moore wrote a School History of North Carolina, from 1584 to the present time, shown here in a revised and enlarged edition. In the preface to the revised edition Moore notes that a fourteenth edition makes it proper to say something as to changes made in the work. At a session of the North Carolina Board of Education on November 22, 1881, the board resolved that it expressly reserved the right to require further revisions in Moore's history. The second edition had then been adopted for use in the public schools. Conforming to that requirement, Moore says, he diligently sought aid and counsel to perfect the work.

Moore names his helpers with care. The work is indebted for many valuable suggestions to Mrs. C. P. Spencer, to E. J. Hale of New York, and to Hon. Montford McGehee, Commissioner of Agriculture. Still larger thanks go to Col. W.
speech-of-mr-cushing-of-massachusetts-on:
Mr. Cushing of Massachusetts spoke in the House on January 25, 1836. His theme was the right of petition. The pleas at hand asked an end to slavery in the District of Columbia. They asked an end to the slave trade there as well. Gales and Seaton printed the speech at Washington that year. Cushing holds several such pleas in his hand. He moves that one of them be received.

The plea he presents prays for both ends at once. Its terms are mild and free of insult. Folk of Haverhill, Massachusetts, signed it. Cushing knows some of the signers by name. He vouches for them as sound and stirred by duty. They are his own voters. They sent the plea to him for placing. Much as he shunned the task, he will not hang back. Each American has the right to be heard, he holds.
the-diamond-cross-mystery-being-a-somewh: Chester K. Steele, author of The Mansion of Mystery, bills The Diamond Cross as a somewhat different detective story, printed in Cleveland in 1918 by the International Fiction Library. Its contents list twenty-two chapters, from The Ticking Watch and King's Dagger through The Diamond Cross itself, an indictment, Singa Phut, The Hidden Wires, Amy's Test, and His Last Case. Only the front matter, contents, and the heading of Chapter I are present here.
the-gifts-of-asti:
Andrew North wrote The Gifts of Asti as a tale of a dying world, first placed in Fantasy Book in 1948. Asti, a god, and Varta, the last of his maidens, stand at the start.

Varta stands on a black terrace by Asti's last shrine and smells the burning of Memphir, the great trade city below. Shaggy warriors of Klem hunt its folk to slow deaths. Beside her crouches Lur, a scaled, mute creature whose golden eyes speak in her mind. More than a thousand years ago Asti left soft Memphir for the hills. Now Varta, the last to sing his dawn hymn, must take his gifts and flee.
the-harvard-classics-volume-49-epic-and-:
The Harvard Classics Volume 49, Epic and Saga, was edited by Charles W. Eliot and published in 1910. The volume holds The Song of Roland, in a translation by John O'Hagan, and The Destruction of Da Derga's Hostel, each with introductions and notes. An introductory note traces Roland back to a real attack in the Pyrenees on August 15, 778.

The note explains how the tale grew over time. Basque attackers gave way to Saracens in the poem, Charlemagne became an old man with a white beard, and a seven-year campaign replaced the short raid of 777-778. Treachery by Ganelon was added to explain the defeat. Readers can see how a brief event became a national epic.
the-kingdom-of-god-is-within-you-christi:
Constance Garnett translated Tolstoi's religious testament from the Russian. This New York edition dates from 1894. Its subtitle calls Christianity a new theory of life. It is not a mystic religion here. Her preface calls the book a remarkable study. Few studies of the modern world's condition match it, she says. Its influence will be lasting and far reaching, she predicts.

Garnett notes the odd reception of Tolstoi's later works. They were much talked about because they were his. They were never seriously discussed, she complains. This volume will end that neglect, she thinks. One may disagree with his views, she writes. Nobody can deny their originality, boldness, and depth. The novelist's art lives inside the prophet's argument. His study of oppressors and oppressed shows it best. So does his account of authority's intoxication.
the-life-of-michelangelo-buonarroti: John Addington Symonds wrote his life of Michelangelo Buonarroti and dedicated it to Guido Biagi of the Laurentian Library. Only the title page and detailed contents are present here, tracing birth and Florentine youth to 1492, the David years, the Sistine vault painting, the siege of Florence, and the Last Judgment. Separate chapters judge Michelangelo as craftsman, architect, poet, and man of feeling. The biography itself cannot be seen in this record beyond that plan.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol:
Additional Poems, 1837 to 1848, form this section of The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes in the 1893 three-volume set. The titles show a young poet in demand for occasions. They include songs for Harvard's centennial and for the Boston dinner given to Charles Dickens on February 1, 1842. Lines for the Berkshire Jubilee appear, and verses for a New York temperance dinner in November 1842.

The section opens with The Pilgrim's Vision. In the hour of twilight shadows a Pilgrim father looks out from his freezing cabin. He thinks of the dangers said to lurk around him. The verse names Wituwamet's pictured knife and Pecksuot's whooping shout. It sets the father's stout arms against the feeble limbs of his baby. Holmes mixes such historical balladry with after-dinner pieces like Nux Postcoenatica and A Rhymed Lesson.
the-underground-railroad-a-record-of-fac: William Still's Underground Rail Road was published in Philadelphia by Porter and Coates in 1872 and sold only by subscription. Only the title page is present in this record, so the narratives do not appear. The title page promises facts, narratives, and letters about enslaved people's hardships, narrow escapes, and death struggles for freedom. Still is named as a longtime worker in the Philadelphia anti-slavery office and chairman of its Acting Vigilant Committee. The page also advertises seventy fine engravings and portraits from photographs.
the-united-empire-loyalists-a-chronicle-:
W. Stewart Wallace wrote The United Empire Loyalists for the Chronicles of Canada series, edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton. Published at Toronto in 1914, it forms volume thirteen of thirty-two. The subject is the great migration of Americans who stayed loyal to Britain during the Revolution.

Wallace opens by charging that Loyalist history was written by their enemies for nearly a century. English writers avoided the subject, early American accounts ignored the Loyalists or painted them black, and he aims to correct the record. Contents chapters trace persecution, service under arms, the exodus to Nova Scotia, new settlements in Quebec and the west, and later compensation.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Eighth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime is a short passage in the United Nations manual printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. It tells how the topic reached the world stage. The Eighth Congress met in 1990. Canada brought a draft text on computer crime with twenty-one backers.

The Congress told states to refresh their crime laws for the machine age. Old offences and proof rules should stretch to cover the new acts. Where gaps show, new bans and search powers should be built. Gains from such crimes should be seized or paid back. Judges and police need training, and the public needs warning. Victims should get fair treatment and be urged to report. The vote also called for work toward shared world rules.
